stories.headline: Man Found Shot Dead on Aurora Sidewalk; No Suspects Identified
stories.summary:
Aurora police are investigating a homicide after a 49-year-old man was found dead with a gunshot wound on a sidewalk near East Warren Avenue and South Galena Street in the city's Dayton Triangle neighborhood. Officers responded shortly before 7:30 a.m. Sunday to a report of an unresponsive male; investigators believe the man had been shot hours earlier.

The victim's identity has not been released and will be determined by the Arapahoe County Coroner's Office. As of Sunday afternoon, no suspects had been publicly identified or arrested.

The case is being handled by the Aurora Police Department's Major Crime Homicide Unit. Anyone with information is asked to contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867.

stories.headline: Denver Moves to Shut Down Five Points Nightclub After Security Guard Accused of Sexual Assault at Gunpoint
stories.summary:
Denver city officials are moving to close a Five Points nightclub following accusations that a security guard sexually assaulted a patron at gunpoint on the premises. The action represents a significant public safety intervention targeting a licensed establishment in one of Denver's historic entertainment districts.

The case highlights ongoing concerns about security oversight at Denver nightlife venues and the city's authority to revoke operating licenses in response to alleged violent crimes committed by staff. Details about the specific nightclub and the status of any criminal charges against the security guard were not immediately available.

City officials have cited the severity of the alleged offense as grounds for the closure action. The move comes as Denver continues to grapple with safety issues in its entertainment corridors.

stories.headline: Nearly 500 Flights Delayed at DIA as Severe Thunderstorm Watch Covers Denver Metro and Eastern Plains
stories.summary:
Severe thunderstorm watches across most of the Denver area and Eastern Plains caused widespread flight disruptions at Denver International Airport on Sunday, with 490 flights delayed and six canceled as of 4:30 p.m. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground delay for DIA, with average holdovers of 29 minutes and the longest delays expected between 5:30 and 7 p.m.

Southwest Airlines led all carriers with 179 delayed flights, followed by SkyWest with 126 and United with 114. Frontier, American Airlines and Delta also reported significant delays. Cancellations included three United flights, two Southwest flights and one Frontier flight.

The severe thunderstorm watch covered 25 counties across eastern Colorado, including Adams, Arapahoe, Denver and Douglas. Forecasters warned of hail up to the size of ping pong balls, 70 mph winds and frequent lightning. Delays were expected to continue into the evening hours.

stories.headline: Two Drownings in Nine Days at Eleven Mile Reservoir Prompt Water Safety Warnings
stories.summary:
Two men have drowned at Eleven Mile Reservoir in Park County within nine days of each other, prompting urgent water safety warnings from state and county officials. In the most recent incident on Friday, two men fell from a shared paddleboard; a bystander rescued one, but the second man, 28, drowned. A life jacket was present but not being worn, officials said.

The earlier drowning on Aug. 6 claimed a 67-year-old man whose kayak flipped in high winds on the reservoir. The Park County Coroner's Office will identify both victims and determine causes of death.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife and the Park County Sheriff's Office are urging all water recreationists to wear properly fitted life jackets, stay sober, monitor weather conditions and keep watch over fellow members of their group. Alcohol and weather are believed to have been factors in the more recent incident.

stories.headline: Man Dies After Being Swept Away by Floodwaters Near Pueblo County Burn Scar
stories.summary:
A man died Sunday after being swept away by fast-moving floodwaters near the Aspen Acres burn scar in Pueblo County, according to officials. Heavy rainfall triggered the dangerous flood conditions in the area, which remained vulnerable to runoff due to fire-damaged terrain that limits water absorption.

Burn scars from wildfires significantly increase flash flood risk by removing vegetation and altering soil composition, causing water to move rapidly across the landscape with little warning. The fatality underscores the compounding dangers facing communities near active or recent wildfire areas during Colorado's monsoon season.

No additional details about the victim were immediately available. The incident adds to a string of flood-related emergencies across Colorado's south metro and surrounding counties in recent days.

stories.headline: Climber Falls 500 Feet from North Maroon Peak, Rescued by Army Helicopter
stories.summary:
A climber sustained multiple injuries Sunday after falling approximately 500 feet while ascending the north face of North Maroon Peak, a fourteener southwest of Aspen in the Maroon Bells Wilderness. Mountain Rescue Aspen responded to the scene, and an Army helicopter from a nearby training site airlifted the climber from the mountain shortly after 2:30 p.m.

The climber was transported by ambulance to a hospital after the helicopter landed at the Aspen airport. The extent of the injuries was not immediately available, and the climber has not been publicly identified.

In a separate incident the same day, a paraglider and a hang glider collided midair over Aspen Mountain, injuring both. One person declined further medical care after being evaluated on scene, while the second required a stretcher rescue involving nearly three dozen Mountain Rescue Aspen crew members. Pitkin County sheriff's officials urged mountain aviation participants to maintain appropriate separation from other aircraft and carry reliable communications and safety equipment.

stories.headline: Denver Sues Major Tobacco Companies Over Cigarette Butt Litter, Seeking Infrastructure Cleanup Costs
stories.summary:
Denver has filed a lawsuit against several of the world's largest tobacco companies — including Philip Morris USA, Altria Group and Liggett Vector Brands — seeking to recover the costs of repairing and maintaining city infrastructure damaged by discarded cigarette filters. Mayor Mike Johnston framed the litigation as an environmental and public decency issue, saying it is "past time Big Tobacco cleaned up the big mess it's created."

City officials explicitly stated they are not pursuing damages for smoking-related health costs, focusing instead on the financial burden of cigarette litter on city maintenance crews and public spaces. The suit alleges violations of public nuisance, trespass, negligence and product liability laws based on how consumers dispose of their products.

Denver's action follows a similar lawsuit filed by Baltimore against the tobacco industry. Defendants have argued in the Baltimore case that extending liability to manufacturers for consumer littering behavior would create untenable legal precedent affecting producers of a wide range of consumer goods.

stories.headline: 'Smoking-Gun' Email Links Trump Administration Directly to Retaliation Against Colorado, Federal Judge Says
stories.summary:
A federal court last week revealed an email from a White House deputy assistant that Colorado officials say directly links the Trump administration's actions against the state to its campaign to free convicted election official Tina Peters. The email, sent under the heading "brainstorm call" by Emily Underwood, notified officials from five federal agencies to prepare "immediate actions" their departments could take regarding Colorado.

Colorado has an ongoing lawsuit against the Trump administration alleging the state has been targeted for retaliation after declining to comply with presidential pressure to release Peters, who was convicted of tampering with election equipment. A federal judge characterized the memo as incompatible with the norms of "our democracy."

The Trump administration has refused to turn over records and documents sought by the state in the litigation. Peters has since been released from prison following a sentence reduction by Gov. Jared Polis and has dined with President Trump at the White House.

stories.headline: Drought Exposes Ruins of Towns Submerged Beneath Colorado's Shrinking Reservoirs
stories.summary:
As Colorado's reservoirs continue to recede amid severe drought conditions, the ruins of towns and ranches deliberately flooded decades ago during dam construction are reemerging above the waterline. At Blue Mesa Reservoir — the state's largest — stone foundations, old roadbeds and structural remnants of communities displaced by the federal government are now visible to visitors willing to explore the exposed lakebed.

Local historian David Primus, author of "Beneath Blue Mesa," has documented the history of communities erased when the Bureau of Reclamation constructed the reservoir. Houses were relocated, graves were exhumed and entire families were uprooted — many refusing to witness the flooding of lands where they had built their lives. Some descendant communities still gather annually.

The emerging ruins raise enduring questions across five major Colorado reservoirs about the tradeoffs between water storage, hydropower and flood control on one hand, and the cultural and human costs of displacement on the other. The Colorado Sun reports similar remnants are surfacing at multiple sites around the state as water levels remain historically low.

stories.headline: DU Students Join National Effort to Combat Senior Isolation Through Intergenerational Pairing Program
stories.summary:
The University of Denver's chapter of Perfect Pair, a national nonprofit that matches college students with older adults to address social isolation, has been connecting students and seniors in the Denver metro area since its founding in 2023 — the first such chapter in Colorado. A second chapter recently launched at Colorado School of Mines, expanding the program's reach across the state.

The organization pairs participants based on shared interests identified through surveys, with the goal of building genuine intergenerational connections. DU social work graduate student Riley Tippit described regular visits with her match, an 86-year-old Englewood woman living in an assisted living facility, as mutually enriching.

Colorado's rapidly aging population has elevated social isolation as a public health concern, with researchers linking chronic loneliness among older adults to increased risks of cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease and premature death. Perfect Pair's model, which emphasizes consistent one-on-one relationships, is part of a broader national push to address the issue through community-based volunteer programs.

stories.headline: Broncos Defensive Backs Coach Doug Belk Brings College Pedigree to Denver's Elite Secondary
stories.summary:
Doug Belk, 38, is beginning his first NFL season as the Denver Broncos' new defensive backs coach after an extensive college football career that included a national championship at Alabama under Nick Saban and coordinator stints at Houston and USC. Belk told the Denver Gazette he had declined earlier NFL opportunities in favor of building his college coaching résumé before making the jump to the professional level.

Belk inherits one of the league's most talented defensive backfields, headlined by cornerback Pat Surtain, the 2024 NFL Defensive Player of the Year. The unit also includes starting safeties Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga, nickel cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian and second-year corner Jahdae Barron, the No. 20 overall pick in 2025.

Belk has emphasized relationship-building during training camp, and early player feedback has been positive. Surtain said the mutual exchange of knowledge between the new coaching staff and veterans has been productive, while cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine noted Belk's commitment to individual player development.

stories.headline: Avalanche Face Pivotal Offseason Question as Artturi Lehkonen Enters Final Contract Year
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche face a significant roster decision with forward Artturi Lehkonen entering the final year of his contract, creating uncertainty about the team's core makeup heading into the 2026-27 NHL season. Lehkonen has been a key contributor to the Avalanche since joining the team, playing an important role in their 2022 Stanley Cup championship run.

The situation adds to a broader set of offseason challenges for Colorado's front office as the team attempts to remain competitive in the Western Conference while managing salary cap constraints. Whether the Avalanche pursue a contract extension, allow Lehkonen to play out the year, or explore trade options will be among the most closely watched decisions of the coming months.

The uncertainty around Lehkonen's future reflects larger questions about the Avalanche's roster construction as the team's championship core continues to age. General manager Chris MacFarland will face pressure to resolve the situation before it becomes a distraction during the regular season.

topStory.headline: Trump Orders Pentagon to Scale Back U.S.-South Korea Military Exercises, Cites Kim Relationship and Iran Dispute
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that he has directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, hours before the annual drills were scheduled to begin. Trump, posting on his Truth Social platform, said the exercises are costly, largely funded by the United States, and send a signal that is "totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea. He said it was too late to cancel the exercises outright but ordered them significantly scaled back.

Trump cited two reasons for the decision: his self-described "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and South Korea's refusal to join U.S. efforts to denuclearize Iran. "Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea," Trump wrote. He acknowledged the Iran rationale was "somewhat unrelated" to the military exercises but raised it nonetheless. The announcement came less than 24 hours after Trump posted a 2019 photograph of himself with Kim, describing the two as great friends.

South Korea's defense ministry said Monday that the drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield and scheduled to run through August 27, were "proceeding as planned." The office of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the two countries had maintained close coordination and expressed hope that the friendly relationship between Trump and Kim would lead to meaningful U.S.-North Korea dialogue. Seoul also noted it had actively participated in international discussions on a ceasefire in Iran and was consulting with Washington on potential military contributions related to the Strait of Hormuz.

The Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises involved approximately 18,000 South Korean soldiers and about 28,500 American military personnel stationed on the peninsula. U.S. and South Korean military leaders had held a joint press conference the previous week announcing the drills, describing them as similar in scale to prior years and noting that training accounted for the threat posed by North Korean troops returning from combat in Ukraine. North Korea's foreign ministry had condemned the exercises Friday as a "rehearsal for an aggressive war" and threatened unspecified retaliation, rhetoric typical ahead of major allied drills.

Defense analysts warned the decision carries significant strategic risk. Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul, said the exercises are essential for military readiness, and that scaling them back could damage alliance coordination, slow South Korea's assumption of greater defense responsibilities, and weaken deterrence in the region. Easley added that cost savings from downsizing the drills are marginal while diplomatic benefits with North Korea remain uncertain. Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, most recently in 2019, and has expressed interest in resuming those discussions since returning to office.
